overview: The Cox–Ross–Rubinstein tree replaces the continuous lognormal world with a lattice of up and down moves, calibrated so the discrete world converges to Black–Scholes as steps multiply. Its pedagogical gift is making risk-neutral pricing concrete: at every node there is an explicit probability q — not a forecast, but the unique weighting that makes the discounted stock a fair game — and the option value is just expectations rolled backward through the lattice. Its practical gift arrives later: unlike the closed form, the tree can ask 'would you exercise here?' at every node, which is exactly what American options and callable bonds need.
formula_latex: u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}, \quad d = \tfrac{1}{u}, \quad q = \frac{e^{(r-\delta)\Delta t} - d}{u - d}, \quad V_t = e^{-r\Delta t}\big[q V_{up} + (1{-}q) V_{down}\big]

variables.name: Move factors
variables.why_it_matters: Chosen so one up-down step reproduces the lognormal variance σ²Δt. The whole calibration of the tree lives in these two numbers.

variables.name: Risk-neutral probability
variables.why_it_matters: The heart of the method. If q left (0,1) the lattice would contain an arbitrage; watching it sit near ½ and drift with (r−δ) builds real intuition for risk-neutral measure.

variables.name: Step size
variables.why_it_matters: Controls the accuracy/effort trade-off: error shrinks roughly like 1/n, with a characteristic odd-even oscillation around the true price as the strike weaves between terminal nodes.

variables.name: Node value
variables.why_it_matters: Backward induction in one line: tomorrow's two values, probability-weighted and discounted. Insert a comparison with immediate exercise here and you have priced an American option.

assumptions: Same economic world as Black–Scholes: constant volatility and rates, no jumps, frictionless trading.
Price moves to exactly two states per step — harmless in the limit, visible at small step counts.
Steps are equally spaced in time.
limitations: Convergence oscillates: adding one step can briefly worsen the price as the strike shifts relative to the terminal grid.
Cost grows with steps (O(n²) node visits); Greeks from finite differences on the tree are noisier than analytic ones.
Inherits every economic limitation of Black–Scholes — the smile and jump critiques apply unchanged.
when_to_use: Whenever exercise decisions matter: American options, callable and puttable bonds, employee stock options. Also as the clearest classroom demonstration of risk-neutral valuation.
when_not_to_use: Plain European payoffs in production — the closed form is faster and exact within the same assumptions. High-dimensional or path-dependent payoffs, where trees explode and Monte Carlo takes over.
industry_usage: Standard for American-style equity options and convertibles; the mental model quants reach for when explaining derivatives pricing to anyone.
computational_complexity: O(n²) in time steps; this laboratory uses n = 500, converging to the closed form within a few tenths of a basis point.
comparison_note: Differences from Black–Scholes shrink roughly like 1/n and oscillate: as steps are added, the strike weaves between terminal nodes and the tree price hops from one side of the closed form to the other. At 500 steps expect agreement within a few tenths of a basis point. A persistent gap would appear only for features the closed form cannot see — early exercise, which this European payoff does not have.
